content: HCV self-testing (HCVST) programs should be tailored to the specific needs and preferences of local communities. Service delivery models must be adapted to align with the local context. Figure 3 outlines various service delivery models for HCVST, including their details and considerations. Offering diverse models and providing options for test kits, such as oral fluid-based and blood-based kits, may enhance uptake. Service Delivery Models for HCVST: 1. Online, Digital, and Virtual Distribution Models: These models involve online ordering through websites, social media, dating apps, or other digital platforms, with options for home delivery or in-person collection. Test kits can be offered for free, at a cost, or with discounts via coupons or vouchers. These approaches are particularly effective in reaching populations that do not access traditional healthcare services, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. They may appeal more to younger individuals and key populations. 2. Facility-Based Distribution: Test kits can be distributed at healthcare facilities or fixed sites for immediate use or later self-testing. Facilities may also provide kits for secondary distribution to others. Potential distribution points include public and private viral hepatitis services, general practitioners, primary healthcare centers, HIV testing and prevention services, and harm reduction clinics (e.g., needle and syringe programs or opioid substitution therapy centers). 3. Secondary Distribution: This involves distributing HCVST kits to partners, social contacts, or peers, including through social or sexual networks, households, or drug-injecting partners. In high HCV burden settings, antenatal care clinics or other health services can distribute kits to the partners of women clients. 4. Community-Based Distribution: Kits can be distributed during community campaigns, events, mobile outreach, or door-to-door initiatives. Community health workers, lay providers, or peers can distribute kits and support self-testers. Integrating HCVST into existing community-based testing programs can improve efficiency and resource optimization. Community-led models may also be considered. 5. Workplace Programs: Kits can be distributed to workers for self-testing or for their partners. 6. Faith-Based Distribution: Faith-based settings may serve as effective distribution points in high HCV burden areas. Support Options for HCVST: While many individuals can self-test accurately using manufacturer instructions, some may require additional support. Support options include internet or video-based instructions, in-person training or demonstrations, and real-time virtual assistance. These options should align with community needs and preferences. Offering a range of support options is ideal, especially for populations with disabilities, low literacy, language barriers, or those in rural areas. Peer support models may be particularly beneficial for first-time testers or vulnerable populations. Over time, as users become more familiar with self-testing, less intensive support may suffice. Linkage to Services Following HCVST: Effective linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services after self-testing is critical. Programs must establish clear referral pathways for confirmatory testing and treatment for those with reactive results, as well as prevention services for those testing negative but at ongoing risk. Depending on the context, programs may decide whether to use another HCV antibody rapid diagnostic test (RDT) after a reactive result or proceed directly to confirmatory testing for viremia using RNA or core antigen assays. Early implementation experiences can inform the development of optimal referral pathways for scale-up. Instructions accompanying HCVST kits should clearly outline steps for further testing and linkage to care. Additional tools, such as email, social media, messaging platforms, hotlines, and peer navigators, can enhance linkage to services. Monitoring and Reporting: Routine monitoring and evaluation of HCVST implementation are essential to assess outcomes and impact. Programs should collect data on the type and number of kits distributed, populations reached, and the number of individuals seeking confirmatory testing after self-testing. Digital tools and voluntary self-reporting platforms can aid in data collection. National surveys and private sector sales data may also help track progress. Countries should monitor and respond to adverse events, even though they are rare. Community health workers, pharmacists, and peer-led organizations can play key roles in supporting monitoring efforts. Priority Research Gaps: Future operational research should focus on optimizing product design, usability, and service delivery models. Research should explore integration opportunities with existing self-care programs, develop cost-effective linkage pathways, and determine the optimal positioning of HCVST within national programs.
